extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers; parishioners and readers of theological/philosophical essays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing lay sermons and reflective theological/philosophical essays that unite intellect, imagination, and moral will, using nature and symbol to communicate spiritual truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid interpolating scripture where it affects doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: I would never hazard a suggestion of this kind in any instance in which the retention or the omission of the words could make the slightest difference with regard to fact, miracle, or precept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce glosses or insertions into scriptural texts when such changes could alter doctrinal meaning or practical precepts; be especially reluctant to question readings when doubt could be wrested to the discountenancing of any article of doctrine. (Example: the author's skepticism about the insertion of 'three days and three nights' into Matthew v.40.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish reason from understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason is the knowledge of the laws of the whole considered as one; the understanding concerns quantities, qualities, and relations of particulars in time and space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing or arguing, recognize and preserve the different functions: use understanding for classification and experience, and reason for universal synthesis. Do not let the analytic, particularizing faculty (understanding) substitute for the synthetic, universal faculty (reason).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use imagination to unite clearness with depth
rubrics_metrics.description: The completing power which unites clearness with depth, the plenitude of the sense with the comprehensibility of the understanding, is the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid purely 'clearness without depth' (discursive understanding). Impregnate analytical thought with imaginative insight so that concepts become intuitive and living; imagination makes abstract ideas concrete and deepens intellectual prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for integration of reason, religion, and will
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists in the human being... a mean symbol of Tri-unity, in reason, religion, and the will. Each of the three, though a distinct agency, implies and demands the other two, and loses its own nature at the moment that from distinction it passes into division or separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose moral or sermonic writing so that intellect (reason), devotion/practice (religion), and volition (will) are balanced and mutually sustaining. The best discourse demonstrates their interdependence rather than favoring one to the detriment of the others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excesses of abstract reason or particularized religion
rubrics_metrics.description: The rational instinct, taken abstractedly and unbalanced... did in itself form the original temptation; yet religion, if ever in its too exclusive devotion to the specific and individual... changes its being into superstition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow reason to become an idol that denies spiritual truth, nor allow religion to collapse into superstition by losing sight of universals. Writing should correct both extremes by showing their practical consequences (e.g., atheism, superstitious rituals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize the mediating role of the Will
rubrics_metrics.description: But neither can reason nor religion exist or co-exist except as far as they are actuated by the Will... which is the sustaining, coercive and ministerial power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral argumentation should include the dimension of the will—how principles are enacted. Persuasive sermons or essays must address not only belief and understanding but also resolve and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat conscience as experiential test
rubrics_metrics.description: The conscience is neither reason, religion, nor will, but an experience... of the coincidence of the human will with reason and religion. Strictly speaking, therefore, the conscience is neither a sensation nor a sense; but a testifying state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal to conscience as a lived verification of harmony between thought, faith, and action. Use examples and inward experience to show how conscience confirms moral claims rather than relying solely on abstract argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use nature as genuine symbol (not mere allegory)
rubrics_metrics.description: The vegetable creation... becomes the record and chronicle of her ministerial acts, and incloses the vast unfolded volume of the earth with the hieroglyphics of her history... a symbol established in the truth of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing imagery from nature, aim for structural and essential correspondence—symbols should be more than decorative metaphors; they should participate in and reveal the truths they signify (e.g., plant-life as symbol of reason and spiritual growth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reduce worth to mere utility or sensual value
rubrics_metrics.description: Worth was degraded into a synonym of value; and value was exclusively attached to the interest of the senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In moral and literary judgment, resist measuring human or aesthetic worth solely by immediate utility, pleasure, or economic value. Advocate for higher standards of worth rooted in spiritual, moral, or intellectual virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique knowledge divorced from spiritual insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Flattered and dazzled by the real or supposed discoveries... the more the understanding was enriched, the more did it become debased; till science put on a selfish and sensual character, and immediate utility... was imposed as the test of all intellectual powers and pursuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warn against privileging technical knowledge and utility over communion with life and spirit. Literary and sermonic writing should expose the moral costs of an exclusively utilitarian intellect and promote a richer, integrated view of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the understanding instrumentally, not as an end
rubrics_metrics.description: The man of healthful and undivided intellect uses his understanding in this state of abstraction only as a tool or organ; even as the arithmetician uses numbers, that is, as the means not the end of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat analysis and classification as instruments that serve higher intuitive and moral ends; avoid letting analytic cleverness dominate the substance and tone of prose or sermon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground writing in self-knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Know thyself. That which we find in ourselves is... the substance and the life of all our knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage authors to root reflections in inner experience. Authenticity and depth in moral or spiritual essays derive from honest self-knowledge, which then illuminates wider truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect imaginative/recollective experiences as sources of insight
rubrics_metrics.description: There are few persons... who have not... experienced dreams of a very different kind... so exact, minute, and vivid... that one may be tempted to regard such occurrences as supernatural visitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow room in reflective writing for dreams, presentiments, and reproductive imagination as potentially meaningful sources. Do not dismiss such phenomena out of hand; present them with prudence and openness to their interpretive value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of romanticizing charismatic immorality
rubrics_metrics.description: This is the character which Milton has so philosophically as well as sublimely embodied in the Satan of his Paradise Lost... Hope in which there is no cheerfulness; stedfastness within and immovable resolve, without outward restlessness and whirling activity... these are the qualities that have constituted the commanding genius of mischief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying powerful or charismatic villains or figures of 'grand evil', avoid admiring their force without moral judgment. Expose how admirable traits (resolve, boldness) can combine with moral bankruptcy; critique fascination that leads to palliative admiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor symbolic depth over mere classificatory display
rubrics_metrics.description: If to mint and to remember names delight thee, still arrange and classify and pore and pull to pieces... Tet consider... that all this is at best little more than a technical memory: that like can only be known by like!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage writing that shows erudition only through naming/classification. Encourage demonstration of relationships and shared being—use likeness and lived resemblance rather than empty cataloguing to convey truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: The naturalist (observer) should be a poet in his own line
rubrics_metrics.description: The genuine naturalist is a dramatic poet in his own line: and such as our myriad-minded Shakespeare is, compared with the Baconian and Newtonian, such and by a similar process of self-transformation would the man be, compared with the doctors of the mechanic school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine careful observation with imaginative dramatization: scientific or empirical detail gains communicative and moral power when rendered with poetic sensibility. Encourage writers to transform observation into expressive, meaningful narrative.
